segments.english: He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; therefore it is said, Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD.
segments.literal: he-was mighty-of hunting before the-LORD on-so it-is-said like-Nimrod mighty-of hunting before the-LORD

tokens.note: nifal imperfect: "it will be said", of a proverbial saying

phrases.literal: 'mighty-of hunting': גִּבּוֹר is construct before צַיִד
'to-the-face-of the LORD'; the English keeps the phrase open (Rashi: in defiance; Ibn Ezra: in worship; Radak and Sforno: intensifier)

grammar: גִּבֹּר־צַיִד is a construct chain: 'mighty one of hunting'.
יֵאָמַר is nifal imperfect: 'it will be said', a proverbial formula, here with the saying quoted after כְּ.
The etnaḥta on יְהוָה divides the verse into the statement about Nimrod and the proverb it explains.
The saying repeats the first half, with כְּנִמְרֹד replacing הוּא הָיָה.
segments.note: The Hebrew leaves the sense of לִפְנֵי יהוה open. The English keeps the words and does not choose. Rashi reads it as defiance: Nimrod trapped people's minds with his words and led them to rebel, and 'before the LORD' means he meant to provoke Him to His face. Ibn Ezra, calling his reading the plain sense, takes it that he built altars and offered the game as burnt offerings to God. Radak and Sforno read it as an intensifier ('exceedingly mighty'). Ramban quotes Rashi and the Sages and rejects Ibn Ezra, but his own reading is that Nimrod was the first to rule over men by force, a hunter of beasts as well, with 'before the LORD' as hyperbole: none under heaven was his equal in might. Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that 'it is said' introduces a proverb.

commentary.summary: Rashi: צָד דַּעְתָּן שֶׁל בְּרִיוֹת בְּפִיו, he trapped people's minds with his speech and led them to rebel against God; so the hunting is figurative. The English says only 'hunter'.
Rashi: מִתְכַּוֵן לְהַקְנִיטוֹ עַל פָּנָיו, he intended to provoke Him to His face. The English keeps 'before the LORD' without choosing this sense.

Rashi: of any man who is brazenly wicked, knowing his Master and intending to rebel against Him, people will say 'like Nimrod, a mighty hunter'. The English follows him in taking the verb as a proverb formula.

Ibn Ezra: the sense of לפני ד' is that he built altars and offered the animals up as burnt offerings to God (עולה לשם, 'to the Name'); this is the way of the plain sense (דרך הפשט), and the midrash goes another way. Recorded as an alternative.
Ibn Ezra: מָשָׁל הָיָה גַם בִּימֵי משה, it was a proverb even in Moses' time. The English follows in presenting the clause as a saying.
Radak: לפני ה' magnifies the might, as in 'a great city to God' (Jonah 3:3); the English does not adopt this.
Sforno: 'very mighty', like עיר גדולה לאלהים; recorded as the intensifier reading.

apparatus: Onkelos renders גִּבֹּר צַיִד as גִּבַּר תַּקִּיף, 'a mighty man', with no word for hunting, and לִפְנֵי יְהוָה as קֳדָם יְיָ, 'before the LORD'. Radak takes this rendering as support for his reading of the verse as praise of Nimrod's might.

segments.english: The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Akkad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.
segments.literal: and-was beginning-of his-kingdom Babel and-Erech and-Akkad and-Calneh in-land-of Shinar

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, feminine singular to agree with רֵאשִׁית

phrases.english: The beginning of his kingdom was
phrases.literal: 'and-was beginning-of his-kingdom'; the wayyiqtol opens the verse as narrative

grammar: וַתְּהִי is feminine because it agrees with the subject רֵאשִׁית, not with the predicate list.
The list is joined with ו before each name after the first; the English uses commas and a final 'and'.
The etnaḥta falls after כַּלְנֵה and sets בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר apart as the location of all four.
segments.note: The pronominal suffix of מַמְלַכְתּוֹ refers to Nimrod, the subject of verses 8 to 9. No normative comment is anchored to this verse.

segments.english: From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah,
segments.literal: from-the-land the-that went-out Asshur and-he-built (object-mark) Nineveh and (object-mark) Rehoboth Ir and (object-mark) Calah

tokens.note: qatal, not wayyiqtol, because the phrase מִן־הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא stands before the verb
wayyiqtol of בנה, a root with final ה: the short form וַיִּבֶן stands for the long form יִבְנֶה
'city'; part of the name or a common noun

phrases.literal: 'went-out Asshur'; Rashi and Ibn Ezra take Asshur as a person
'and (object mark) Rehoboth Ir'; 'wide places of a city' or the name Rehoboth-Ir

grammar: מִן־הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא is placed before the verb, so the departure from Shinar is emphasised.
אַשּׁוּר is a personal name here (the subject of וַיִּבֶן), though it is also the name of the land.
Each city is marked with אֶת; the repeated אֶת־ divides the list.
The merkha on רְחֹבֹת and tipḥa on עִיר show the two words are read together.
segments.note: אַשּׁוּר may be read as the land (to Asshur he went out, i.e. 'he went out to Assyria', Ramban). The English takes it as the person who went out, as Rashi and Ibn Ezra do. Whether עִיר is part of the name Rehoboth-Ir or means 'the wide streets of the city' (that is, of Nineveh) is left open. The final comma leaves the list to continue into verse 12.

commentary.summary: Rashi: when Asshur saw his sons obey Nimrod and rebel against God by building the tower, he left their midst. The English follows in taking Asshur as the subject who went out from that land.

Ibn Ezra: Asshur is a son of Japheth (sic, in the text as printed); this was after the division of the earth, and Nimrod was the first king over Babel. The English follows in taking Asshur as a person who left; Ramban's reading of the verb as 'Nimrod went out to Asshur' is not adopted.

apparatus: Ramban takes Nimrod as the subject of 'went out' and אַשּׁוּר as his destination, 'he went out to Asshur', since Asshur was of the sons of Shem (10:22). He cites verbs of motion with a bare accusative of the goal, without ה of direction (Num 34:4; Deut 3:1), and Micah 5:5, which calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod'. Radak takes Asshur as the subject, of Ham or of Shem.

segments.english: and Resen, between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city.
segments.literal: and (object-mark) Resen between Nineveh and-between Calah she the-city the-great

tokens.note: attributive adjective: it follows הָעִיר and agrees with it in gender (feminine), number and the article. None of the senses listed in the entry is 'great' in size, so no sense is given.

phrases.literal: 'between Nineveh and-between Calah'; בֵּין is repeated before each term
'she the-city the-great'; the pronoun is the copula

grammar: בֵּין is repeated before each term, as normal in Hebrew.
הִוא הָעִיר הַגְּדֹלָה is a verbless clause; the feminine pronoun agrees with עִיר.
The etnaḥta after כָּלַח separates this clause from the preceding list.

The grammar does not fix the pronoun's antecedent: Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as Nineveh, the first city built (10:11); Ibn Ezra allows Resen or Calah; Radak takes it as Resen, the city the verse is speaking of.
segments.note: The antecedent of הִוא is ambiguous. Rashi takes it as Nineveh, citing Jonah 3:3; Ibn Ezra prefers Nineveh and allows Resen or Calah. Radak, against 'most commentators', takes it as Resen. The English keeps the pronoun as 'that' and does not name the city; the reading of the normative commentators, Nineveh, is the one the edition takes.

commentary.summary: Rashi: הִיא נִינְוֵה, as it says 'Nineveh was an exceedingly great city to God' (Jonah 3:3). The English leaves the antecedent open in wording, though agreeing with this reading.

Ibn Ezra: the reading closest to his view is that the clause joins 'and he built Nineveh', so the great city is Nineveh; to join it to Resen or to Calah is not far-fetched either. The English leaves the pronoun open in its wording and allows his preferred reading.

apparatus: Whether הִוא refers to Nineveh, Resen or the group Nineveh-Resen-Calah is disputed; Ibn Ezra allows Resen or Calah.

segments.english: And Egypt fathered the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim,
segments.literal: and-Egypt he-fathered (object-mark) Ludim and (object-mark) Anamim and (object-mark) Lehabim and (object-mark) Naphtuhim

tokens.note: the name Mizraim, in the dual form
qal of ילד with a male subject: 'begot'

grammar: The subject מִצְרַיִם comes before the verb, which begins the genealogy of Ham's son.
All four names are plural gentilics in -ִים, so they name peoples, not single persons.

The pazer on מִצְרַיִם and the gershayim on יָלַד are disjunctive. In the list the tevir on עֲנָמִים and the tipḥa on לְהָבִים divide the names; the darga on לוּדִים is conjunctive and binds it to the next word.
The list continues in verse 14.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra's observation that these are all plural (names of regions, each region a family) means 'fathered' is used loosely of peoples. The English keeps 'fathered' and the plural names, with the Hebrew name Mizraim given as Egypt per decisions.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the Lehabim are so called because their faces are like a flame (לַהַב). A derivation of the name; it does not bear on the English.

Ibn Ezra: these are names of countries, in each of which is a family, so all are plural; the proof is that the Philistines went out from there and שם refers to a place. The English follows by writing the names as plural peoples.

apparatus: The BDB entry glosses נַפְתֻּחִים as 'the northern land' and כַּפְתֹּרִי as 'Cretans'; these are data from the lexicon, not decisions of the English.

segments.english: the Pathrusim, the Casluhim, from whom the Philistines came, and the Caphtorim.
segments.literal: and (object-mark) Pathrusim and (object-mark) Casluhim which went-out from-there Philistim and (object-mark) Caphtorim

tokens.note: perfect, plural, with the Philistines as subject

phrases.literal: 'which went-out from-there Philistim'; אֲשֶׁר ... מִשָּׁם is a relative with a resumptive adverb, so 'from there' becomes 'from whom'

grammar: אֲשֶׁר ... מִשָּׁם is a relative clause with a resumptive adverb: 'which ... from there'.
The relative clause may attach to Pathrusim and Casluhim together or only to the second; the revia on כַּסְלֻחִים closes the pair.
The Philistines follow the verb as subject: 'went out from there, the Philistines'.
The verse ends the Mizraite list with Caphtorim, set after the parenthesis.
segments.note: The relative clause is ambiguous in attachment. Rashi takes it as 'from both', the Philistines coming from the Pathrusim and Casluhim together; the English leaves the antecedent as the pair. The Caphtorim stand after the parenthesis. Ibn Ezra says that Mizraim fathered the Caphtorim too, and explains why ילד is said of a father: the son comes from the father's vigour and strength, in his image and likeness.

commentary.summary: Rashi: מִשְּׁנֵיהֶם יָצְאוּ, the Philistines came from both, since the Pathrusim and Casluhim exchanged their wives' beds. The English follows on the antecedent (both) but not on the explanation.

Ibn Ezra: Egypt also fathered the Caphtorim, and because the son comes from the father's strength and likeness, one says 'fathered' of him. The English keeps 'and the Caphtorim' as a further object of fathered in verse 13.

apparatus: The Philistines are named in the verse as coming from the Casluhim (Amos 9:7 and Jeremiah 47:4 say Caphtor), a known difficulty; the English does not harmonize.
